In [[mathematics]], the '''Bretherton equation''' is a [[nonlinear partial differential equation]] introduced by [[Francis Bretherton]] in 1964:<ref name=Bretherton>{{harvtxt|Bretherton|1964}}</ref>

:<math>u_{tt}+u_{xx}+u_{xxxx}+u = u^p,</math>

with <math>p</math> [[integer]] and <math>p \ge 2.</math> While <math>u_t, u_x</math> and <math>u_{xx}</math> denote [[partial derivative]]s of the [[scalar field]] <math>u(x,t).</math>

The original equation studied by Bretherton has [[quadratic function|quadratic]] nonlinearity, <math>p=2.</math> [[Ali H. Nayfeh|Nayfeh]] treats the case <math>p=3</math> with two different methods: [[Gerald B. Whitham|Whitham's]] [[averaged Lagrangian]] method and the [[method of multiple scales]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Nayfeh|2004|loc=§§5.8, 6.2.9 & 6.4.8}}</ref>

The Bretherton equation is a model equation for studying weakly-nonlinear [[dispersion (water waves)|wave dispersion]]. It has been used to study the interaction of [[harmonic]]s by [[nonlinear resonance]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Drazin|Reid|2004|pages=393–397}}</ref><ref>{{citation | title = Resonant interactions among surface water waves | first1 = J.L. | last1 = Hammack | first2 = D.M. | last2 = Henderson | author2-link = Diane Henderson | year = 1993 | journal = Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics | volume = 25 | pages = 55–97 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.fl.25.010193.000415 |bibcode = 1993AnRFM..25...55H }}</ref> Bretherton obtained analytic solutions in terms of [[Jacobi elliptic function]]s.<ref name=Bretherton/><ref>{{harvtxt|Kudryashov|1991}}</ref>

==Variational formulations==
The Bretherton equation derives from the [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] density:<ref>{{harvtxt|Nayfeh|2004|loc=§5.8}}</ref>

:<math>
  \mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 \left( u_t \right)^2 + \tfrac12 \left( u_x \right)^2 -\tfrac12 \left( u_{xx} \right)^2 
              - \tfrac12 u^2 + \tfrac{1}{p+1} u^{p+1}
</math>

through the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]]:

:<math>
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u_t} \right)
  + \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u_x} \right)
  - \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \left( \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u_{xx}} \right)
  - \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u} = 0.   
</math>

The equation can also be formulated as a [[Hamiltonian system]]:<ref name=Levandosky>{{citation |title = Decay estimates for fourth order wave equations | journal = Journal of Differential Equations | volume = 143 | issue = 2 | pages = 360–413 | year = 1998 | doi = 10.1006/jdeq.1997.3369 | first = S.P. | last = Levandosky |bibcode = 1998JDE...143..360L | doi-access = free }}</ref>

:<math> 
\begin{align}
  u_t & - \frac{\delta{H}}{\delta v} = 0,
  \\
  v_t & + \frac{\delta{H}}{\delta u} = 0,
\end{align}
</math>

in terms of [[functional derivative]]s involving the Hamiltonian <math>H:</math>

:<math> H(u,v) = \int \mathcal{H}(u,v;x,t)\; \mathrm{d}x </math> {{pad|2em}} and {{pad|2em}} <math>
  \mathcal{H}(u,v;x,t) = \tfrac12 v^2 - \tfrac12 \left( u_x \right)^2 +\tfrac12 \left( u_{xx} \right)^2 
                       + \tfrac12 u^2 - \tfrac{1}{p+1} u^{p+1}
</math>

with <math>\mathcal{H}</math> the Hamiltonian density – consequently <math>v=u_t.</math> The Hamiltonian <math>H</math> is the total energy of the system, and is [[conservation law|conserved]] over time.<ref name=Levandosky/><ref>{{citation | journal=Communications in Theoretical Physics | volume=55 | issue=3 | first=A. | last=Esfahani | year=2011 | doi=10.1088/0253-6102/55/3/01 | pages=381–386 | title=Traveling wave solutions for generalized Bretherton equation |bibcode = 2011CoTPh..55..381A | s2cid=250783550 }}</ref>
